title: Symmetry Operations as Matrices
lead: Each symmetry operation of a group can be written as a matrix acting on a chosen basis, such as the unit vectors along x, y and z or a set of atomic orbitals. The set of these matrices is a matrix representation of the group.
notes: Written by Claire Vallance and Jerry LaRue and shared under CC BY 4.0, with nothing left out.
exercise_notes: The section prints no exercises; the one on the matrix of S₄ is new and AI-written, with its answer checked by multiplying the matrices. Its Bloom level and concept tags were chosen by AI.

exercises.source_id: The inverse of a rotation matrix is another rotation matrix
exercises.prompt: The improper rotation $S_4$ about $z$ is a $C_4$ rotation about $z$ followed by a reflection in the $xy$ plane. Write the matrix of $S_4$ acting on $\mathbf{u} = (x, y, z)$ by multiplying the matrices of the two operations, then square it. Which single operation is $S_4^2$?

answer.hint: With $n = 4$ the rotation matrix has $\cos 90^\circ = 0$ and $\sin 90^\circ = 1$.
answer.solution:
With $\cos 90^\circ = 0$ and $\sin 90^\circ = 1$, the rotation is $C_4 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, and reflecting afterwards multiplies on the left by $\sigma(xy)$:

$$ S_4 = \sigma(xy)C_4 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} $$

Squaring it,

$$ S_4^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} $$

which is the matrix of $C_2$ about $z$: $(x, y, z) \rightarrow (-x, -y, z)$. Two quarter turns make a half turn, and the two reflections in the $xy$ plane cancel.

footnotes.html: The usual wording, and Vallance's own, runs the other way: the basis spans the representation.

Equation 12.4.4 puts $-\sin\theta$ at the top right and $+\sin\theta$ at the bottom left, which is a turn by $-\theta$. A counterclockwise turn by $\theta$ about $y$, in the same sense as $R_x$ and $R_z$, is $R_y(\theta) = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & 0 & \sin\theta \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\sin\theta & 0 & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix}$.

$\sigma_v'$ is the plane through the middle carbon at right angles to the molecule, so it carries $p_1$ onto $p_3$ and $p_3$ onto $p_1$. In both displays $\sigma_v'$ takes $(p_1, p_2, p_3)$ to $(p_3, p_2, p_1)$, which is what the printed matrix $\Gamma(\sigma_v')$ gives.
